newsitem.title: USA: Plaintiffs rest case in Fla. Reynolds trial.
newsitem.headline: Plaintiffs rest case in Fla. Reynolds trial.

text.p: The plaintiffs in a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co rested their case on Wednesday with a brief videotape of smoker Jean Connor taken days before her death.

Jurors who will decide whether Reynolds bears any responsibility for Connor's death were allowed to see the one-minute video clip over the objections of lawyers for the tobacco company, who said it was prejudicial.

The first half of the tape, taken about six weeks before she died, showed a gaunt Connor walking into a bedroom and removing a blonde wig to reveal her bald head -- the effects of chemotherapy. The second half, about a week before her death, showed her taking tiny, feeble steps down a hallway.
Connor, a three-pack-a-day smoker who took up the habit as a teenager, died of lung cancer in October 1995 at age 49.

Attorneys for plaintiff Dana Raulerson, who sued Reynolds on behalf of the estate of her sister and Connor's three children, said they wanted to present the tape to show what the children had to deal with as Connor was dying.

They had initially asked Judge Bernard Nachman to allow jurors to view a longer video, but after watching it for a few seconds, Nachman refused to allow it, saying it was "emotionally overwhelming" to him.
Reynolds' lawyers argued the tape should not be shown because it did not show the suffering of the children.
Nachman allowed the jurors to see the one-minute video clip after ruling it was not inflammatory.
Reynolds began its defense by calling to the witness stand David Townsend, its director of product development and assessment and a specialist in cigarette design.
Townsend testified that the company was concerned about consumer health and constantly researched ways to modify the potential risks of smoking.
"It's the right thing to do ... our customers are concerned about the possible health risks of smoking and we are as well," he said.
Townsend said the most important factor in cigarette design was consumer acceptance, indicating that cigarettes made with lower tar or lower nicotine did not always find a wide following.
"Most of the time, those very unusual cigarettes have limited or no consumer acceptance," he said.
Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
